blocks.content: "Containerization" is the general technique, Docker is simply the most popular tool for doing it. Understanding the technique itself, separate from any one product, is what lets you reason about Docker, Podman, or containerd with the same mental model.

Containerization means taking an application and everything it depends on and sealing them into one isolated, runnable unit. That unit behaves like its own tiny machine from the inside (it has its own filesystem, its own view of running processes, its own network interface), while actually sharing the host machine's kernel with every other container on it.

blocks.alt: App and its dependencies, sealed into one isolated process

blocks.content: 2. Namespaces: The Illusion of a Private Machine
blocks.text: 2. Namespaces: The Illusion of a Private Machine

blocks.content: Linux namespaces are the kernel feature that makes isolation possible. A PID namespace makes a container see only its own processes (it might think its main process is PID 1, even though the host sees it as some ordinary PID). A network namespace gives the container its own network interfaces and routing table. A mount namespace gives it its own view of the filesystem.

blocks.alt: Different namespace types isolate different resources

blocks.content: Isolation alone is not enough, a single misbehaving container should not be able to starve every other container on the host of CPU or memory. Control groups (cgroups), another Linux kernel feature, let the container engine cap exactly how much CPU, memory, and disk I/O each container is allowed to consume.

blocks.alt: cgroups enforce hard limits per container

blocks.content:
docker run --memory="512m" --cpus="1.0" myapp
# This container can never use more than 512MB of RAM
# or more than one full CPU core, enforced by cgroups.

blocks.content: 4. The OCI Standard: Why This Is Not Docker-Specific
blocks.text: 4. The OCI Standard: Why This Is Not Docker-Specific

blocks.content: Namespaces and cgroups are Linux kernel features, not Docker inventions, which is why containerization is not locked to one vendor. The Open Container Initiative (OCI) standardizes the image format and runtime behavior so that an image built by Docker can be run by containerd, Podman, or any other OCI-compliant engine.

Containerization did not begin with Docker. chroot (1979) first let a process see a restricted view of the filesystem. Linux Containers (LXC, 2008) combined namespaces and cgroups into something resembling modern containers. Docker's real contribution in 2013 was not inventing isolation, it was making containers dramatically easier to build, share, and run, through the image format and a simple CLI.

blocks.alt: Docker popularized containers, it did not invent isolation

blocks.title: Key Takeaway
points: Containerization is a general technique built on two Linux kernel features, namespaces for isolation and cgroups for resource limits, Docker is one tool that packages this technique conveniently.
Because the OCI standard governs the image and runtime format, images are portable across container engines, not locked into whichever one built them.
